# TCB Allowed List — Nanvix phys-mm

Any `external_body` outside this list must be removed.

## Allowed `external_body`

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::instance` — materializes a `&'static mut Inner` from the
  module-level `static mut INSTANCE: MaybeUninit<Inner>` singleton (guarded by `INSTANCE_INIT`).
  Raw-memory op over externally-owned `static mut` storage Verus cannot verify without a
  `PointsTo` (mirrors `bump_allocator`/`raw-array`). `ensures` pins the singleton's abstract
  state to `phys_view().frames`, asserts `(*r).inv()`, and records `phys_view().initialized` —
  the §8 ghost-token attachment for the singleton frame allocator.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::clear`
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc` — materializes a
  `&'static mut [u8; N]` from a backend-provided address (`usize as *mut`); raw-memory
  op Verus cannot verify without a `PointsTo` for the externally-owned `BssStorage`
  region. Mirrors `src/libs/raw-array`. `ensures` states alignment + in-bounds over
  the abstract `bump_view`.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc_as` — delegates to
  `alloc` and re-materializes the slot as `&'static mut MaybeUninit<T>`; same rationale.
  `ensures` adds the `size_of::<T>()`/`align_of::<T>()` vs `(N, A)` guard arms.

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`

- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::read` — reads a `TableEntry` from a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *const E::Word`).
  Verus does not support `usize`→pointer casts (int-to-ptr materialization of externally-owned,
  volatile page-table memory), so the body cannot be verified. Same trust-boundary rationale as
  `bump_allocator::alloc` (`usize as *mut`) and `frame::instance`. See
  `nanvix-phys-arch-paging-table/verus-unsupported.md`. **The function is not contract-free:** it
  carries a full `#[verus_spec]` pinned to the global page-table-memory ghost — `requires index@ <
  PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, `ensures result == spec_table_read::<E>(self@.addr, index@)` — exactly as
  `frame::instance` pins its result to `phys_view()` (parameter-free global ghost, no signature
  change).
- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::write` — writes a `TableEntry` into a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *mut E::Word`).
  Same int-to-ptr / volatile externally-owned-memory limitation as `read`. Carries only the sound
  `requires index@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` (auto from `TableIndex::inv`); it has **no** contents
  `ensures`. A contents postcondition pinning the *pure* global ghost `spec_table_word(self@.addr,
  index@)` to the caller-chosen `entry` would be unsound for an `external_body` (assumed)
  contract: two writes of distinct entries to the same slot would assume
  `spec_entry_raw(e1) == spec_entry_raw(e2)`, which with `lemma_entry_roundtrip` derives
  `e1 == e2`, i.e. `false` (Turn 2 review #2/#3/#15; exploit reproduced). The genuine `old@ -> @`
  slot-update transition (`self@.entries[index@] == Some(entry)`, other slots framed) is therefore
  **deferred to the proving-phase page-table permission token**, exactly the `identity_map_view()`
  `v -> v'` deferral convention in `identity_map.spec.rs`.

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `arch::x86::mem::paging` (`mod.rs`)

- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/mod.rs::invlpg` — the body is a single
  `core::arch::asm!` block issuing the `invlpg` instruction, which flushes the CPU TLB
  entry for `vaddr`. Verus does not support inline-asm expressions, so the body cannot be
  verified — an external-bottom hardware trust boundary (same class as the volatile
  page-table access in `table::read`/`write` and the int-to-pointer materialization in
  `frame::instance`/`bump_allocator::alloc`). See
  `nanvix-phys-arch-paging-mod/verus-unsupported.md`. The effect is purely on hardware TLB
  state (outside Verus' memory model and invisible to every caller's Rust-visible state),
  so the faithful contract is **empty**: no `requires` (any `usize` is accepted), trivial

Any `external_body` outside this list must be removed.

## Allowed `external_body`

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::instance` — materializes a `&'static mut Inner` from the
  module-level `static mut INSTANCE: MaybeUninit<Inner>` singleton (guarded by `INSTANCE_INIT`).
  Raw-memory op over externally-owned `static mut` storage Verus cannot verify without a
  `PointsTo` (mirrors `bump_allocator`/`raw-array`). `ensures` pins the singleton's abstract
  state to `phys_view().frames`, asserts `(*r).inv()`, and records `phys_view().initialized` —
  the §8 ghost-token attachment for the singleton frame allocator.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::clear`
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc` — materializes a
  `&'static mut [u8; N]` from a backend-provided address (`usize as *mut`); raw-memory
  op Verus cannot verify without a `PointsTo` for the externally-owned `BssStorage`
  region. Mirrors `src/libs/raw-array`. `ensures` states alignment + in-bounds over
  the abstract `bump_view`.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc_as` — delegates to
  `alloc` and re-materializes the slot as `&'static mut MaybeUninit<T>`; same rationale.
  `ensures` adds the `size_of::<T>()`/`align_of::<T>()` vs `(N, A)` guard arms.

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`

- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::read` — reads a `TableEntry` from a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *const E::Word`).
  Verus does not support `usize`→pointer casts (int-to-ptr materialization of externally-owned,
  volatile page-table memory), so the body cannot be verified. Same trust-boundary rationale as

  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *mut E::Word`).

1. # View Design: `hal::platform::microvm` (`gva_to_gpa`)
2. 
3. In-scope (verification-order) target: the single free function
4. `gva_to_gpa(gva: usize) -> usize` in
5. `src/kernel/src/hal/platform/microvm/mod.rs`. Every other item in the module
6. (the `Platform` struct, `init`, `parse_bootinfo`, the MMIO/control-register
7. helpers, `virt_to_phys`, `is_valid_physical_address`, …) is **out of scope** and
8. left untouched.
9. 
10. ## Abstract Resource
11. 
12. To callers, this slice of the module is the MicroVM platform's
13. **guest-virtual → guest-physical address translation**: a single, pure, total
14. mathematical map over the `usize` address space. On MicroVM the guest runs
15. identity-mapped, so that map *is the identity* (`gpa == gva`).
16. 
17. It is emphatically **not** a collection, a resource manager, or a state machine:
18. 
19. - `gva_to_gpa` is a free function, not a method, and touches **no** module state.
20.   It does not read or write `Platform`, the frame allocator, the page tables, or
21.   any `static mut`. The `Platform` struct is irrelevant to this function.
22. - It is `usize -> usize`, total and infallible (no `Result`/`Option`, no panic,
23.   no trap), and deterministic (output depends only on the argument).
24. 
25. The sole in-tree caller — `book_mmio_regions` in `mm/phys/mod.rs:114` — uses it
26. to reinterpret a frame-aligned virtual MMIO address as the physical frame address
27. that backs it, then feeds the result to `PhysicalAddress::from_mmio_address` and
28. `frame::is_covered` / `frame::book`. The only thing the caller relies on is that
29. the returned GPA corresponds **frame-for-frame** to the input GVA.
30. 
31. ## View Type
32. 
33. There is **no stateful View, and no `impl View` block**, because there is no type
34. under verification and no caller-observable mutable state. `gva_to_gpa` is a pure
35. function; the thing to abstract is the *translation map itself*, not an object's
36. state. This mirrors the `PhysicalAddress` precedent in this codebase, where the
37. abstraction collapsed to a bare `int` rather than a one-field struct once the
38. substitution/minimality tests removed every candidate field.
39. 
40. The abstraction is therefore a single **pure spec function** that names the
41. translation map. It lives in the (currently empty) `mod.spec.rs`:
42. 
43. ```rust
44. // The MicroVM platform's guest-virtual -> guest-physical translation map.
45. //
46. // MicroVM runs the guest identity-mapped, so the abstract map is the identity
47. // over the entire usize address space. This is a platform-level invariant
48. // (the VMM maps GVA==GPA), NOT an implementation artifact: any reimplementation
49. // of the translation on MicroVM must still yield the identity, so the equality
50. // is part of the contract, hence `open`.
51. //
52. // Total: defined for every address. Deterministic: a function of `gva` alone.
53. pub open spec fn spec_gva_to_gpa(gva: int) -> int {
54.     gva
55. }
56. ```
57. 
58. ### Why a spec function over `int`, not a struct (substitution test)
59. 
60. Per the view-design skill (Step 2, *minimize fields*): every field must
61. correspond to a caller-observable abstract concept that would **survive a
62. complete reimplementation**. Running the substitution test over every candidate
63. field rejects all of them, leaving no struct:
64. 
65. | Candidate field | Substitution test | Verdict |
66. |---|---|---|
67. | the input/output address pair | not state — it is the function's argument/result, already named by `spec_gva_to_gpa` | reject (duplicate) |
68. | an offset / base (`gpa = gva + offset`) | encodes one *strategy* (offset map); a real GVA→GPA walk would not have an offset; on MicroVM the offset is fixed at 0 | reject (implementation detail) |
69. | a `Map<int, int>` of translations | a translation is a *total function*, not a stored finite table; materializing it as `Map` invents internal bookkeeping no implementation keeps | reject (code-as-spec) |
70. | `memory_size` / address-space bounds | not consulted by `gva_to_gpa` (it is total over all `usize`); belongs to `is_valid_physical_address` / `max_physical_address`, which are out of scope | reject (wrong function) |
71. | any `Platform` field (`arch`, `physical_memory_layout`, …) | the function never reads `Platform`; including it would be mirroring an unrelated internal struct | reject (caller-invisible / unrelated) |
72. 
73. Nothing remains to put in a struct. The entire caller-observable abstraction is
74. "the translation is the function `g ↦ g`", which a single `open spec fn`
75. expresses directly. Wrapping a lone identity in a struct would add ceremony to
76. every spec with zero gain.
77. 
78. ### `open` vs `closed`
79. 
80. `spec_gva_to_gpa` is `pub open`. The caller (`book_mmio_regions`) must derive
81. **frame correspondence** — that the GPA it books is the frame backing the MMIO
82. GVA — and on MicroVM that fact *is* `result == gva`. Hiding the body behind
83. `closed` would leave the caller unable to prove the booked frame is the right
84. one. Because the identity is a platform-level guarantee (the VMM's identity
85. mapping), exposing it does not leak an implementation choice; it states the
86. contract.
87. 
88. ## Well-formedness Invariant
89. 
90. There is **no instance `inv()`**, because there is no instance: a pure, stateless
91. function carries no well-formedness state to constrain. The standard
92. `pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool` does not apply here.
93. 
94. What plays the role of "well-formedness" is a set of **properties of the map**
95. that every caller relies on. They are not free-standing facts: each is pinned to
96. `gva_to_gpa`'s contract in the spec phase (the only way they prove anything), and
97. each is, for the identity map, trivially discharged:
98. 
99. ```rust
100. // Totality / infallibility: spec_gva_to_gpa is defined for every address, and
101. // the exec function returns it directly with no error/panic path. Captured by
102. // the unconditional (no `requires`) ensures below.
103. 
104. // Determinism / purity: spec_gva_to_gpa is a mathematical function of `gva`
105. // alone — same input yields same output by construction.
106. 
107. // Frame correspondence (the caller's load-bearing property): translating a
108. // frame-aligned address and stepping by FRAME_SIZE yields the matching
109. // sequence of physical frames. For the identity map this is immediate, and it
110. // is *subsumed* by the ensures `result == gva` (advancing the GVA by FRAME_SIZE

 # View Design: `hal::platform::microvm` (`gva_to_gpa`)
 
 In-scope (verification-order) target: the single free function
 `gva_to_gpa(gva: usize) -> usize` in
 `src/kernel/src/hal/platform/microvm/mod.rs`. Every other item in the module
 (the `Platform` struct, `init`, `parse_bootinfo`, the MMIO/control-register
 helpers, `virt_to_phys`, `is_valid_physical_address`, …) is **out of scope** and
 left untouched.
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 To callers, this slice of the module is the MicroVM platform's
 **guest-virtual → guest-physical address translation**: a single, pure, total
 mathematical map over the `usize` address space. On MicroVM the guest runs
 identity-mapped, so that map *is the identity* (`gpa == gva`).
 
 It is emphatically **not** a collection, a resource manager, or a state machine:
 
 - `gva_to_gpa` is a free function, not a method, and touches **no** module state.
   It does not read or write `Platform`, the frame allocator, the page tables, or
   any `static mut`. The `Platform` struct is irrelevant to this function.
 - It is `usize -> usize`, total and infallible (no `Result`/`Option`, no panic,
   no trap), and deterministic (output depends only on the argument).
 
 The sole in-tree caller — `book_mmio_regions` in `mm/phys/mod.rs:114` — uses it
 to reinterpret a frame-aligned virtual MMIO address as the physical frame address
 that backs it, then feeds the result to `PhysicalAddress::from_mmio_address` and
 `frame::is_covered` / `frame::book`. The only thing the caller relies on is that
 the returned GPA corresponds **frame-for-frame** to the input GVA.
 
 ## View Type
 
 There is **no stateful View, and no `impl View` block**, because there is no type
 under verification and no caller-observable mutable state. `gva_to_gpa` is a pure
 function; the thing to abstract is the *translation map itself*, not an object's
 state. This mirrors the `PhysicalAddress` precedent in this codebase, where the
 abstraction collapsed to a bare `int` rather than a one-field struct once the
 substitution/minimality tests removed every candidate field.
 
 The abstraction is therefore a single **pure spec function** that names the
 translation map. It lives in the (currently empty) `mod.spec.rs`:
 
 ```rust
 // The MicroVM platform's guest-virtual -> guest-physical translation map.
 //
 // MicroVM runs the guest identity-mapped, so the abstract map is the identity
 // over the entire usize address space. This is a platform-level invariant
 // (the VMM maps GVA==GPA), NOT an implementation artifact: any reimplementation
 // of the translation on MicroVM must still yield the identity, so the equality
 // is part of the contract, hence `open`.
 //
 // Total: defined for every address. Deterministic: a function of `gva` alone.
 pub open spec fn spec_gva_to_gpa(gva: int) -> int {
     gva
 }
 ```
 
 ### Why a spec function over `int`, not a struct (substitution test)
 
 Per the view-design skill (Step 2, *minimize fields*): every field must
 correspond to a caller-observable abstract concept that would **survive a
 complete reimplementation**. Running the substitution test over every candidate
 field rejects all of them, leaving no struct:
 
 | Candidate field | Substitution test | Verdict |
 |---|---|---|
 | the input/output address pair | not state — it is the function's argument/result, already named by `spec_gva_to_gpa` | reject (duplicate) |
 | an offset / base (`gpa = gva + offset`) | encodes one *strategy* (offset map); a real GVA→GPA walk would not have an offset; on MicroVM the offset is fixed at 0 | reject (implementation detail) |
 | a `Map<int, int>` of translations | a translation is a *total function*, not a stored finite table; materializing it as `Map` invents internal bookkeeping no implementation keeps | reject (code-as-spec) |
 | `memory_size` / address-space bounds | not consulted by `gva_to_gpa` (it is total over all `usize`); belongs to `is_valid_physical_address` / `max_physical_address`, which are out of scope | reject (wrong function) |
 | any `Platform` field (`arch`, `physical_memory_layout`, …) | the function never reads `Platform`; including it would be mirroring an unrelated internal struct | reject (caller-invisible / unrelated) |
 
 Nothing remains to put in a struct. The entire caller-observable abstraction is
 "the translation is the function `g ↦ g`", which a single `open spec fn`
 expresses directly. Wrapping a lone identity in a struct would add ceremony to
 every spec with zero gain.
 
 ### `open` vs `closed`
 
 `spec_gva_to_gpa` is `pub open`. The caller (`book_mmio_regions`) must derive
 **frame correspondence** — that the GPA it books is the frame backing the MMIO
 GVA — and on MicroVM that fact *is* `result == gva`. Hiding the body behind
 `closed` would leave the caller unable to prove the booked frame is the right
 one. Because the identity is a platform-level guarantee (the VMM's identity
 mapping), exposing it does not leak an implementation choice; it states the
 contract.
 
 ## Well-formedness Invariant
 
 There is **no instance `inv()`**, because there is no instance: a pure, stateless
 function carries no well-formedness state to constrain. The standard
 `pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool` does not apply here.
 
 What plays the role of "well-formedness" is a set of **properties of the map**
 that every caller relies on. They are not free-standing facts: each is pinned to
 `gva_to_gpa`'s contract in the spec phase (the only way they prove anything), and
 each is, for the identity map, trivially discharged:
 
 ```rust
 // Totality / infallibility: spec_gva_to_gpa is defined for every address, and
 // the exec function returns it directly with no error/panic path. Captured by
 // the unconditional (no `requires`) ensures below.
 
 // Determinism / purity: spec_gva_to_gpa is a mathematical function of `gva`
 // alone — same input yields same output by construction.
 
 // Frame correspondence (the caller's load-bearing property): translating a
 // frame-aligned address and stepping by FRAME_SIZE yields the matching
 // sequence of physical frames. For the identity map this is immediate, and it
 // is *subsumed* by the ensures `result == gva` (advancing the GVA by FRAME_SIZE
 // advances the GPA by FRAME_SIZE). Stated as a derivable property, not a
 // separate clause:
 //   forall|g: int| spec_gva_to_gpa(g + FRAME_SIZE) == spec_gva_to_gpa(g) + FRAME_SIZE
 // and injectivity:
 //   forall|a: int, b: int| spec_gva_to_gpa(a) == spec_gva_to_gpa(b) ==> a == b
 ```
 
 These are listed as design intent; in the spec phase they collapse to corollaries
 of `result == gva` and need no standalone statement.

 `gva_to_gpa` mutates nothing, so there is no state transition. Its "transition"
 relates the input address to the resulting abstract address, expressed over the
 View's `int` domain via the spec function above. The contract added to the exec
 function is:
 
 ```rust

 // ensures: the result is exactly the platform translation map applied to gva,
 // i.e. the identity on MicroVM. Frame correspondence and infallibility follow.
 pub fn gva_to_gpa(gva: usize) -> (result: usize)
     ensures
         result as int == spec_gva_to_gpa(gva as int),   // == gva
 { ... }
 ```
 
 Equivalently `result == gva`. The indirection through `spec_gva_to_gpa` names the
 platform abstraction (WHAT: "apply the GVA→GPA map") rather than restating the
 body (HOW: "return the argument"), keeping the spec declarative and giving future
 non-identity platforms a single named hook to redefine.
 
 ## Design Rationale
 
 - **Abstraction = the translation map, not an object.** The caller reasons about
   one thing: "what physical frame backs this virtual MMIO address?" The map
   answers exactly that, and nothing in the module's state participates.
 - **One named spec function, `int`-typed.** Minimal (one symbol), abstract
   (`int`, overflow-free — identity cannot overflow anyway), and caller-usable:
   `result == gva` drops straight into `book_mmio_regions`' proof to show the
   booked frame matches the MMIO frame.
 - **No `requires`.** Totality is a caller expectation (the loop calls it with no
   guard); an empty precondition records that faithfully.
 - **`open` body.** Frame correspondence is only provable if the identity is
   visible; the identity is a platform contract, so exposing it is correct, not a
   leak.
 - **Properties subsumed, not multiplied.** Determinism, injectivity, and
   frame-stepping all follow from `result == gva`; per the minimality principle
   they are documented but not emitted as extra ensures clauses.
 
 ## Rejected Alternatives
 
 1. **A `MicrovmView` / `PlatformView` struct with platform state.** Rejected:
    `gva_to_gpa` reads no `Platform` field. Modeling `arch`,
    `physical_memory_layout`, etc. would mirror an unrelated internal struct and
    violate caller-only + minimality.
 2. **An offset field (`gpa = gva + base`).** Rejected by the substitution test:
    it bakes in the "linear offset map" strategy. A real page-walk implementation
    has no single offset; on MicroVM the offset is identically 0, so the field is
    dead. The identity is better stated directly.
 3. **`Map<int, int>` of translations.** Rejected as code-as-spec: a translation
    is a *total function*, and a finite `Map` both misrepresents it (it is defined
    on all of `usize`) and invents bookkeeping no implementation maintains.
 4. **Address-space bounds (`memory_size`, `max_physical_address`) in the View.**
    Rejected: `gva_to_gpa` is total and never consults bounds; range validation is
    the job of `is_valid_physical_address` / `max_physical_address`, which are out
    of scope. Adding bounds here would over-specify and couple unrelated functions.
 5. **`closed` spec function hiding the identity.** Rejected: the caller could no
    longer derive frame correspondence, defeating the only reason the function is
    verified. The identity is a contract, not a hidden detail.
 6. **Separate ensures clauses for injectivity / determinism / frame-stepping.**
    Rejected as subsumed: all are corollaries of `result == gva`; emitting them
    would be redundant (minimality / "subsumed properties" anti-pattern).

===== spec-design =====
---
name: spec-design
description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
---

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
   `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
   functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
   Always search vstd first.
3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
   module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
   `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
   specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
   annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
   for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
   is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
   by vstd.
   **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
   functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
   trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
   verified later, the specs become fully proven.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
   must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
   make Verus pass.
   **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
   with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
   can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.

### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)

1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
   signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
   Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
   erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
   prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
   rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
   genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
   
   Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
   fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
   or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
   spec or proof instead.
   
   **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
   - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
     source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
     crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.

   **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**

   1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
      in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
      `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
      reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
      Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
      requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
   2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
      guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
      guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
      Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
      clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
      callers will not check it.
   3. **Soft contract coverage**: identify semantic contracts that the
      compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
      explicitly in the spec.
   4. **No stronger than the API**: the spec must not assume more than
      the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
      code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"
   5. **Version sensitivity**: note the stdlib/crate version the
      assumption was checked against.

   - `external_body`: allowed on dependency functions in other modules as
     a temporary contract placeholder (removed when that module is verified),
     and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.
     Never use `external_body` on the current module's own functions to skip
     verification.
   
   `assume_specification` and `axiom` are unverified axioms.
   See the audit checklist above when writing `assume_specification`.
3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
   the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
   loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec. Verus will reject
   it. For complex invariants, define a `spec fn` predicate in spec.rs
   or proof.rs and reference it in the `invariant` clause. The invariant
   must be strong enough that, combined with the loop exit condition, it
   implies the function's `ensures`. The invariant may need to be
   strengthened later — that is expected.
4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
   or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
   spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.

   verifies the copy, not the real code.

   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.

   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.

   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.

   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**

   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over

   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.

   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes

name: spec-design
description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
---

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
   `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
   functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
   Always search vstd first.
3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
   module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
   `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
   specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
   annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
   for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
   is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
   by vstd.
   **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
   functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
   trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
   verified later, the specs become fully proven.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
   must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
   make Verus pass.
   **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
   with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
   can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.

1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
   signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
   Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
   erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
   prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
   rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
   genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
   
   Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
   fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
   or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
   spec or proof instead.
   
   **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
   - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose

      requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).

      guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
      guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
      Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
      clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
      callers will not check it.

      compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
      explicitly in the spec.

      the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
      code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"

      assumption was checked against.

     a temporary contract placeholder (removed when that module is verified),
     and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.
     Never use `external_body` on the current module's own functions to skip
     verification.
   
   `assume_specification` and `axiom` are unverified axioms.
   See the audit checklist above when writing `assume_specification`.
3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
   the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
   loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec. Verus will reject
   it. For complex invariants, define a `spec fn` predicate in spec.rs
   or proof.rs and reference it in the `invariant` clause. The invariant
   must be strong enough that, combined with the loop exit condition, it
   implies the function's `ensures`. The invariant may need to be
   strengthened later — that is expected.
4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
   or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
   spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing
   (or `true`) about failure. Error paths need equal rigor.
6. **Missing Frame Condition / Field-by-Field Conjunction** — ensures says
   what changed but not what didn't, OR lists unchanged fields one by one
   (fragile — easy to forget a field). **Always use struct update syntax**
   (`..old(self)@`) so completeness is guaranteed by construction:

   Bad (fragile — silent field omission):
   ```
   self@.field_a == old(self)@.field_a,
   self@.field_b == old(self)@.field_b,
   self@.field_c == new_value,
   // forgot field_d — spec is incomplete!
   ```
   Good (complete by construction):
   ```
   self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
   ```
   This applies everywhere state changes appear in ensures — whether
   inline or via spec transition functions.
7. **Separate Ok/Err Conditions** — using `result.is_ok() ==> ...` and
   `result.is_err() ==> ...` as separate ensures clauses instead of a
   single `match`. The `match` form is complete by construction and
   prevents accidentally omitting one arm:

   Bad:
   ```
   ensures
       result.is_ok() ==> /* success postcondition */,
       result.is_err() ==> self@ == old(self)@,
   ```
   Good:
   ```
   ensures match result {
       Ok(v)  => /* success postcondition */,
       Err(e) => self@ == old(self)@,
   }
   ```
8. **Tautological Postconditions** — trivially true for any return value.
9. **Subsumed Properties** — logically implied by a stronger property
   already present. Before adding an ensures clause, check: is this
   derivable from `self.inv()` combined with the other ensures? If so,
   delete it — redundant clauses obscure the spec's intent and make
   reviews harder.
10. **Over-specification** — forcing a particular implementation strategy.
   Only add specificity when callers genuinely depend on it.
11. **Scattered Invariant** — the same property appears in `requires` of
    every (or nearly every) method. A universally required property is an
    invariant — move it to `inv()` and maintain it in `ensures`.
12. **`uninterp` as Verification Escape** — using `uninterp spec fn` to
    avoid writing a concrete spec definition, then injecting properties
    via `external_body` proof axioms. This combination is equivalent to
    `assume` — it introduces unverified assumptions about a function
    whose behavior is entirely under our control.
    `uninterp spec fn` is banned. All spec functions must have concrete
    definitions. If `uninterp` appears on `View::view()` of an
    `external_body` type, that is a mechanical consequence of the type
    being `external_body` — the trust obligation is tracked there, not
    as a separate `uninterp` allowance. If a spec function is hard to
    define concretely, that is a signal to simplify the abstraction,
    not to use `uninterp`.

### Error Path Spec Principles

with the same rigor as the success path.

2. **Bidirectional Failure Condition** — express error conditions as abstract

   ```
   This makes both arms visible for review — neither path is silently omitted.

- **Boilerplate trait impls** — derived traits, mechanical delegations

   - Preconditions (requires): what must the caller guarantee?

20. - `report -o <dir>` — full report with all diffs
21.

23. from git, or omit both on `verus-ai/*` branches for auto-detection:
24.

27. python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py original.rs verified.rs count
28. 
29. # Via git ref:
30. python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py --base-ref main verified.rs count
31. 
32. # Auto-detect on verus-ai/* branches:
33. python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py verified.rs count
34. ```

40. `ast_report`) with the same auto-detection.
41. 
42. ## Pre-Approved Deviations
43. 
44. These minimal exec changes are known Verus limitations — no full deviation
45. process needed, but still document with a comment:
46. 
47. | Original | Verus Version | Reason |
48. |----------|--------------|--------|
49. | `self.x += 1` | `self.x = self.x + 1` | Compound assignment unsupported |
50. | `self.arr[i] \|= v` | `self.arr.set(i, self.arr[i] \| v)` | Mutable index unsupported |
51. | `-> T` | `-> (ret: T)` | Named returns for ensures |
52. | `#[derive(Clone, ...)]` | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))] #[derive(...)]` | cfg-gating incompatible derives |
53. | `Ok(Self { .. })` | `let result = Self { .. }; Ok(result)` | Ensures needs to reference return value |
54. | `f(complex_expr)` | `let x = complex_expr; f(x)` | Intermediate value for assertions |
55. | `.ok_or_else(\|\| ...)` | `match ... { Some(v) => v, None => return Err(...) }` | Closures unsupported in some contexts |
56. | `v.std_method(args)` | `wrapper(&mut v, args)` | `&mut T` method unsupported; see `verus-constraints` skill for wrapper rules |
57.

59. 
60. Exec changes that fix verified bugs are also pre-approved. These must:
61. - Have a `// VERUS BUG FIX: <description>` comment at the fix site
62. - Be recorded in `bugs.md` with full evidence
63. - Be committed with `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix
64. - Be limited to auto-fixable categories (overflow, off-by-one, missing
65.   bounds check, unchecked cast) — see `bug-reporting` skill
66. 
67. ## Handling MISMATCHes
68. 
69. When the checker reports a MISMATCH:
70. 
71. 1. **Default: restore original code.** Exec changes are violations. Use
72.    `git show <base_ref>:path/to/file.rs` to view the original, then
73.    manually restore the changed exec code while keeping your annotations.
74.    Adapt the proof to the original code — not the other way around.
75. 2. **Check pre-approved deviations.** If the change matches one above,
76.    keep it but add a comment documenting which deviation and why.
77. 3. **Verify it's a real Verus limitation.** Before accepting any other
78.    change, confirm Verus genuinely cannot handle the original construct:
79.    - Search vstd for existing support (e.g. `checked_mul` has vstd specs)
80.    - Try alternative proof strategies that preserve the original code
81.    - Build a minimal reproducer proving the limitation
82. 4. **If confirmed, document with full evidence.** Add a `VERUS DEVIATION`
83.    comment explaining: what was changed, why the original doesn't work,
84.    what alternatives were tried, and why this is the smallest possible change.

     { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
 }
 ```
 
 **Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**
 
 ```rust
 // ❌ WRONG: entire function gated out, replaced with a different definition
 #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
 fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
 #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
 fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
 ```
 
 Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
 meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept.

3. description: "Detect spec weakening via tree-sitter comparison against a baseline SHA. Use in specification, proving, and cheating-elimination phases to enforce that requires/ensures are never silently removed or relaxed."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Spec Drift Check
7. 
8. ## What Is Spec Drift?
9. 
10. Spec drift occurs when a function's `requires` or `ensures` clauses are removed,
11. relaxed, or replaced with weaker versions during a pipeline phase. This is a
12. critical integrity violation because:
13. 
14. - **Callers depend on the spec.** Upstream modules may have already proven their
15.   correctness assuming the original spec. Weakening it silently breaks those proofs.
16. - **Weakening is never acceptable as a proof strategy.** If a spec is hard to
17.   prove, the proof needs strengthening, not the spec weakening.
18. 
19. ## When to Use
20. 
21. Use this skill in **every review** during these phases:
22. - **Specification** — compare phase START baseline → current HEAD
23. - **Proving** — compare specification END → current HEAD
24. - **Cheating Elimination** — compare phase START baseline → current HEAD
25. 
26. ## How to Run
27. 
28. ### Auto-detect mode (recommended)
29. 
30. The `check` subcommand reads `pipeline_state.json` to automatically determine
31. the module, source file, current phase, and baseline SHA:
32. 
33. ```bash
34. python3 scripts/spec_drift.py check <module_name>
35. ```
36. 
37. ### Manual mode
38. 
39. Use `git-diff` when you need explicit control over the comparison range:
40. 
41. ```bash
42. python3 scripts/spec_drift.py git-diff <source_file> --before <baseline_sha> [--after <ref>]
43. ```
44. 
45. Where:
46. - `<source_file>` is the module's source file (relative to repo root)
47. - `<baseline_sha>` is the phase start SHA
48. - `--after` defaults to working tree if omitted
49. 
50. ### Exit Codes
51. - **0** — No contract drift detected ✅
52. - **1** — Contract drift detected ⚠ — spec weakening found
53. - **2** — Fatal error (tool failure)
54. 
55. ### Example
56. 
57. ```bash
58. # Auto-detect from pipeline state
59. python3 scripts/spec_drift.py check libhfs-src-internal-volume_impl
60. 
61. # Manual comparison between two SHAs
62. python3 scripts/spec_drift.py git-diff src/libs/slab/src/lib.rs \
63.     --before abc1234 --after def5678
64. ```
65. 
66. ## What Counts as Contract Drift
67. 
68. | Change | Verdict | Reason |
69. |--------|---------|--------|
70. | `ensures` clause removed | ⚠ FAIL | Callers may depend on it |
71. | `ensures` clause replaced with weaker version | ⚠ FAIL | Reduces verification value |
72. | `requires` clause added | ⚠ FAIL | Shifts proof burden to callers |
73. | `requires` clause strengthened | ⚠ FAIL | Callers may not satisfy it |
74. | Spec/proof function body changed | ⚠ FAIL | May change meaning of specs |
75. | Dependency spec fn body changed | ⚠ FAIL | Effective contract of callers changed |
76. | Top-level entry spec changed vs base branch | ⚠ HARD FAIL | Never allowed — verification target |
77. | Function with specs removed | ⚠ FAIL | Callers lose verified contract |
78. | `recommends` clause changed | ⚠ FAIL | May weaken soft preconditions |
79. | New `ensures` clause added | ✅ OK | Strengthens the contract |
80. | `requires` clause removed/relaxed | ✅ OK | Relaxes precondition for callers |
81. | Proof body changed (same spec) | ✅ OK | Only proof strategy changed |
82. 
83. ## Reviewer Checklist Item
84. 
85. When reviewing, verify:
86. 
87. 1. **Run the command.** Do not skip — check exit code.
88. 2. **If exit code 1:** Read the report. For each weakened function:
89.    - Is the original spec genuinely incorrect? If so, replace it with an
90.      equally strong (not weaker) correct spec.
91.    - Is this a proof difficulty workaround? **FAIL** — demand the
92.      original spec be restored and proven.
93. 3. **Document.** Record the drift check result in your review output.
94. 
95. ## Incorrect Spec vs Weakening
96. 
97. If a spec is genuinely wrong (e.g., encodes an incorrect formula or references
98. wrong fields), correct it. Note: if the code cannot satisfy a caller-required
99. spec, that is likely a **code bug**, not an incorrect spec. The correction must:
100. 1. Be equally strong — fix the error, do not weaken
101. 2. Still satisfy all caller expectations from `caller_analysis.md`
102. 
103. Weakening is **never** acceptable:
104. - "The proof is too hard" → strengthen the proof, not weaken the spec
105. - "Verus can't handle this" → use lemmas, external proof, or escalate
106. - "The caller doesn't actually need this" → the caller wrote their proof
107.   assuming the spec; removing it breaks their proof silently
108. 
109. ## Transitive Spec Drift
110. 
111. A function's effective contract includes the bodies of spec functions called
112. in its `requires`/`ensures`. The drift checker tracks these transitively
113. and flags `EFFECTIVE CONTRACT CHANGED` when a dependency spec fn
114. body is modified. Review these with the same rigor as direct clause changes.
115. 
116. ## Top-Level vs Internal Spec Drift
117. 
118. The pipeline distinguishes two levels of drift checking:
119. 
120. **Top-level entry point specs** are the functions listed in the verification
121. plan's `entries` field. These are always compared against the base branch.
122. Any change is a hard FAIL with no auto-fix.
123. 
124. **Internal module specs** are intermediate artifacts created to prove
125. top-level specs. The drift policy for internal specs:
126. 
127. - **Strengthening** (weaker precondition, stronger postcondition) is fine —
128.   this is normal refinement during proving.
129. - **Weakening** an existing spec may break callers further up the chain.
130.   If weakening is necessary, run a full `make verify` (not just the current
131.   module) to check that all callers still verify. If a caller breaks, adjust
132.   the caller to accommodate the change while still satisfying the top-level
133.   spec.
134.

1. ---
2. name: spec-design
3. description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Spec Design Guide
7. 
8. ## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles
9. 
10. ### Qualities of a Good Spec
11. 
12. 1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
13.    `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
14.    functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
15. 2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
16.    exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
17.    copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
18.    verifies the copy, not the real code.
19. 3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
20.    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
21.    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
22. 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
23.    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
24.    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
25. 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
26.    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
27.    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
28.    recursive spec functions.
29. 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
30.    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
31.    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
32.    type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
33.    If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
34. 7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
35.    over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
36.    `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
37.    addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
38.    non-negative and bounded by the address space.
39. 8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
40.    writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
41.    this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
42.    unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
43.    directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
44.    (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
45.    `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
46.    vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
47.    implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
48.    and return values through the module's public spec interface,
49.    `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.
50. 
51. ### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria
52. 
53. If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
54. nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
55. spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
56. design model.
57. 
58. 1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
59.    by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
60.    module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
61.    and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
62.    annotation beats no annotation.
63. 2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
64.    provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
65.    `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
66.    functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
67.    Always search vstd first.
68. 3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
69.    module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
70.    `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
71.    specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
72.    annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
73.    for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
74.    is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
75.    by vstd.
76.    **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
77.    functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
78.    trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
79.    verified later, the specs become fully proven.
80. 5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
81.    connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
82. 6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
83.    must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
84.    make Verus pass.
85.    **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
86.    with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
87.    can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.
88. 
89. ### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)
90. 
91. 1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
92.    struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
93.    signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
94.    Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
95.    erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
96.    prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
97.    rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
98.    genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
99.    
100.    Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
101.    fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
102. 2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
103.    or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
104.    spec or proof instead.
105.

 # Spec Design Guide
 
 ## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles
 
 ### Qualities of a Good Spec
 
 1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
    `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
    functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
 2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
    exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
    copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
    verifies the copy, not the real code.
 3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
    recursive spec functions.
 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
    type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
    If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
 7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
    over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
    `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
    addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
    non-negative and bounded by the address space.
 8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
    writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
    this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
    unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
    directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
    (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
    `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
    vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
    implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
    and return values through the module's public spec interface,
    `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.
 
 ### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria
 
 If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
 nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
 spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
 design model.
 
 1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
    by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
    module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
    and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
    annotation beats no annotation.
 2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
    provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
    `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
    functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
    Always search vstd first.
 3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
    module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
    `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
    specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
    annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
    for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
    is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
    by vstd.
    **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
    functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
    trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
    verified later, the specs become fully proven.
 5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
    connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
 6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
    must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
    make Verus pass.
    **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
    with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
    can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.
 
 ### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)
 
 1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
    struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
    signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
    Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
    erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
    prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
    rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
    genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
    
    Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
    fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
 2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
    or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
    spec or proof instead.
    
    **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
    - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
      source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
      crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.
 
    **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**
 
    1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
       in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
       `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
       reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
       Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
       requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
    2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
       guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
       guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
       Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
       clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
       callers will not check it.
    3. **Soft contract coverage**: identify semantic contracts that the
       compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
       explicitly in the spec.
    4. **No stronger than the API**: the spec must not assume more than
       the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
       code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"
    5. **Version sensitivity**: note the stdlib/crate version the
       assumption was checked against.
 
    - `external_body`: allowed on dependency functions in other modules as
      a temporary contract placeholder (removed when that module is verified),
      and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.
      Never use `external_body` on the current module's own functions to skip
      verification.
    
    `assume_specification` and `axiom` are unverified axioms.
    See the audit checklist above when writing `assume_specification`.
 3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
    the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
    loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec. Verus will reject
    it. For complex invariants, define a `spec fn` predicate in spec.rs
    or proof.rs and reference it in the `invariant` clause. The invariant
    must be strong enough that, combined with the loop exit condition, it
    implies the function's `ensures`. The invariant may need to be
    strengthened later — that is expected.
 4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
    or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
    spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
 5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing
    (or `true`) about failure. Error paths need equal rigor.
 6. **Missing Frame Condition / Field-by-Field Conjunction** — ensures says
    what changed but not what didn't, OR lists unchanged fields one by one
    (fragile — easy to forget a field). **Always use struct update syntax**
    (`..old(self)@`) so completeness is guaranteed by construction:
 
    Bad (fragile — silent field omission):
    ```
    self@.field_a == old(self)@.field_a,
    self@.field_b == old(self)@.field_b,
    self@.field_c == new_value,
    // forgot field_d — spec is incomplete!
    ```
    Good (complete by construction):
    ```
    self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
    ```
    This applies everywhere state changes appear in ensures — whether
    inline or via spec transition functions.
 7. **Separate Ok/Err Conditions** — using `result.is_ok() ==> ...` and
    `result.is_err() ==> ...` as separate ensures clauses instead of a
    single `match`. The `match` form is complete by construction and
    prevents accidentally omitting one arm:
 
    Bad:
    ```
    ensures
        result.is_ok() ==> /* success postcondition */,
        result.is_err() ==> self@ == old(self)@,
    ```
    Good:
    ```
    ensures match result {
        Ok(v)  => /* success postcondition */,
        Err(e) => self@ == old(self)@,
    }
    ```
 8. **Tautological Postconditions** — trivially true for any return value.
 9. **Subsumed Properties** — logically implied by a stronger property
    already present. Before adding an ensures clause, check: is this
    derivable from `self.inv()` combined with the other ensures? If so,
    delete it — redundant clauses obscure the spec's intent and make
    reviews harder.
 10. **Over-specification** — forcing a particular implementation strategy.
    Only add specificity when callers genuinely depend on it.
 11. **Scattered Invariant** — the same property appears in `requires` of
     every (or nearly every) method. A universally required property is an
     invariant — move it to `inv()` and maintain it in `ensures`.
 12. **`uninterp` as Verification Escape** — using `uninterp spec fn` to
     avoid writing a concrete spec definition, then injecting properties
     via `external_body` proof axioms. This combination is equivalent to
     `assume` — it introduces unverified assumptions about a function
     whose behavior is entirely under our control.
     `uninterp spec fn` is banned. All spec functions must have concrete
     definitions. If `uninterp` appears on `View::view()` of an
     `external_body` type, that is a mechanical consequence of the type
     being `external_body` — the trust obligation is tracked there, not
     as a separate `uninterp` allowance. If a spec function is hard to
     define concretely, that is a signal to simplify the abstraction,
     not to use `uninterp`.
 
 ### Error Path Spec Principles
 
 Every function that can fail should specify **what happens on failure**
 with the same rigor as the success path.
 
 1. **State Preservation** — on error, the state must not change.

221. 2. **Bidirectional Failure Condition** — express error conditions as abstract
222.    predicates on the module's interface state, not as a list of individual
223.    code checks. Ask: what condition at the interface level makes success
224.    impossible?
225. 3. **Liveness** — if the preconditions and current state make success
226.    possible, the spec must guarantee success (i.e., the function must
227.    not spuriously return `None`/`Err`). A spec that *allows* failure
228.    even when success is achievable is under-specified — callers cannot
229.    rely on it. Use `match` on the return value to specify both arms:
230.    ```
231.    ensures match result {
232.        Ok(v)  => /* success postcondition */,
233.        Err(e) => /* error postcondition */,
234.    }
235.    ```
236.    This makes both arms visible for review — neither path is silently omitted.
237. 
238. ### Where NOT to Invest Spec Effort
239. 
240. **Completely skip** (no spec needed at all):
241. - **Type-system guarantees** — ownership, borrow rules, type matching
242. - **Display/formatting** — debug output, logging, string representation
243. - **Boilerplate trait impls** — derived traits, mechanical delegations
244. 
245. **Basic ensures only** (no additional spec design):
246. - **Trivial accessors** — field getters still need
247.   `ensures result == self@.field` for callers to reason about, but
248.   warrant no further properties.
249. - **Pure wrappers** — functions that directly delegate to a single
250.   verified function with no additional logic.
251. 
252. ### Property Coverage Checklist
253. 
254. When writing specs, systematically cover these four dimensions for each
255. function and type. This ensures no important properties are missed.
256. 
257. 1. **Functional Correctness** — What does the code achieve?
258.    - Preconditions (requires): what must the caller guarantee?
259.    - Success postconditions (ensures, Ok case): new abstract state, return value, frame condition
260.    - Error postconditions (ensures, Err case): state preservation, failure condition in abstract terms
261. 
262. 2. **Safety** — What must never happen?
263.    - Bounds, disjointness, uniqueness, conservation, injectivity, ordering, monotonicity
264. 
265. 3. **Liveness** — What good things must happen?
266.    - Guaranteed success conditions, resource availability, recoverability
267. 
268. 4. **Structural Consistency** — Is the data self-consistent?
269.    - Type invariants, field relationships, valid ranges
270. 
271. ### Invariant Design
272. 
273. Two kinds of invariants appear during specification:
274. 
275. - **Type invariant (`inv()`)** — defined on the View type (see **view-design**
276.   skill). Every constructor must establish it; every method must preserve it.
277.   If a property appears in `requires` of nearly every method, it belongs in
278.   `inv()` instead.
279. - **Loop invariant** — defined on loops. Must hold on entry (base case),
280.   be preserved by each iteration (inductive step), and together with the
281.   exit condition imply the function's `ensures` (sufficiency). Define
282.   complex invariants as `spec fn` predicates rather than inline clauses.
283. 
284. Both should reference View fields and abstract state, not implementation
285. details.
286. 
287. ### Static vs Dynamic Condition Enforcement
288. 
289. **Key question**: Can this runtime check be statically eliminated through
290. verification?
291. 
292. **Yes → add `requires`**. The condition is provable from caller context
293. (e.g., index bounds derived from loop invariants, capacity checked before
294. insertion). The runtime check serves as a safeguard during development;
295. once all callers are verified, it becomes dead code and can be removed.
296. 
297. **No → keep runtime check + Err**. The condition depends on inherently
298. dynamic information (external input, hardware state, concurrent
299. operations) that no amount of static reasoning can discharge. A
300. `requires` clause here would be unsound or unusable.
301. 
302. **Guideline**: When both `requires` and a runtime check coexist, the
303. runtime check is a temporary safety net. Mark it as removable (e.g.,
304. `// TODO: remove once all callers are verified`) so that future
305. verification work knows to clean it up.
306. 
307. ### Post-Generation Spec Refinement
308. 
309. After writing ensures clauses, review each one through the caller's eyes.
310. The guiding question: **could a caller who has never seen the implementation
311. find every ensures clause natural and directly useful?**
312. 
313. 1. **Substitution test** — would this clause survive a reimplementation
314.    that preserves abstract behavior but changes internal strategy? If not,
315.    it encodes implementation detail and should be rewritten or removed.
316. 2. **Minimality** — does this clause add information beyond what the other
317.    clauses already imply? Remove anything derivable from the rest.
318. 3. **Direct usability** — can the caller use this clause as-is in their
319.    proof, or must they transform it first? If the latter, provide the
320.    form the caller actually needs.
321.

324. ## Part 2: Spec Classification
325. 
326. Specifications fall into three categories with different ownership:
327. 
328. ### Internal
329. 
330. Specs that exist solely to help the verifier: helper lemmas, loop
331. invariants, intermediate assertions, proof-function pre/postconditions.
332. **The AI generates these freely during proving.** The test for
333. correctness is whether the code above can use them — the verifier
334. provides direct feedback.
335. 
336. ### External-top (API contracts)
337. 
338. Public function `requires`/`ensures`, type invariants exposed to
339. callers, View types. These define **what the module promises**.
340. 
341. ### External-bottom (trust assumptions)
342. 
343. Assumptions about layers below the verification scope: std library
344. behavior, hardware semantics, runtime correctness, compiler fidelity.
345. These are unverified: if they do not match reality, downstream proofs
346. may be unsound. Mechanisms include `assume_specification`,
347. `external_body`, and `axiom`. Which functions belong in this category
348. is pre-determined by the TCB allowed list — do not make new trust
349. boundary decisions during specification or proving.
350. 
351. ### Rules
352. 
353. - The caller analysis and View design identify external-top properties.
354. - Trust boundary decisions (which functions get `external_body`) are
355.   pre-approved in the TCB allowed list. Do not classify new functions
356.   as trust boundaries — if a function is not in the list, it must be
357.   fully verified.
358. - When writing `assume_specification`, follow the audit checklist in
359.   Part 1 (Anti-Patterns, Verification Escape).
360. 
361. ---
